content:
Rachel Kim: collecting CSM questions for LTS FAQ. can folks drop the top Qs you’re getting from enterprise + any suggested wording? trying to have something we can hand to CSMs for pilots + new deals.

Jasmine Liu: +1. support is already getting “what’s the SLA on security fixes” and “can we request backports for perf regressions?”

Avery Johnson: Deal side: customers keep asking for a single sentence commitment. e.g. “6-12 month stable baseline, monthly patches.” Need exact language we can use without overcommitting.

Hannah Schmitt: Also: “does LTS mean no change?” and “do i still need to upgrade when mainline ships CVEs?”

Liam O'Rourke: TAM Q: “how do we pin versions in Private (installer/Helm) and how do we roll back?” — they want steps + how to verify artifact integrity.

Soojin Lee: marketing angle: we should define what LTS is / isn’t. I can help tighten language, but need technical details (cadence, backport policy, support window).

Talia Benson: here’s a doc stub I started for the FAQ (WIP): https://confluence.redwoodinference.com/display/CS/runtime-lts-faq-draft
please paste Qs + suggested answers in-thread and I’ll consolidate.

Connor O'Brien: dropping the current intended commitments (please keep phrasing precise):
- LTS is a maintained runtime release line with a fixed baseline (kernel + scheduling stability focus)
- patch cadence: monthly patch releases (e.g. 1.18.1-lts, 1.18.2-lts), plus out-of-band security fixes when needed
- backports eligible: security, Sev1 correctness/crash, Sev2 high-impact correctness. not feature work.
- each patch goes through CI + perf gates; we’ll include perf deltas + known issues in release notes
- support window target: 12 months from initial LTS branch cut (exact dates published per line)

Rachel Kim: perfect. I’ll start drafting answers. adding Q list:
1) What is Runtime LTS?
2) How often do patches ship?
3) What changes can land in LTS (backport policy)?
4) How do customers request a backport?
5) Security response: what’s covered and how fast?
6) Are patches mandatory?
7) Compatibility: hosted/dedicated/private + model compatibility matrix
8) How do we pin/roll back (Private)?
9) Release notes: what to expect

Dev Patel: For #4 (request backport), please require some minimum info so we don’t thrash:
- affected runtime version + deployment mode (Dedicated/Private)
- severity (crash/data correctness/perf regression)
- repro steps or logs (at least request id + model + prompt length distribution)
- business impact + workaround
We should point to a Support intake form / ticket template.

Jasmine Liu: yes. also add “what if it’s only happening in customer env” — answer should say we’ll try to reproduce, may request diagnostic bundle, etc.

Hannah Schmitt: customer question verbatim from today: “If we adopt LTS, do we get bug fixes automatically or do we have to upgrade each month?”

Connor O'Brien: they still need to upgrade to consume fixes (we’re not auto-updating private). Dedicated/Hosted we can roll within customer-approved windows depending on contract; LTS just reduces churn and makes changes predictable.

Avery Johnson: can we propose standard answer:
- Hosted: Redwood controls runtime, customer pins model versions, LTS applies to runtime under the hood for eligible tenants
- Dedicated: Redwood coordinates upgrades w/ customer-approved maintenance windows; option to stay on a specific LTS patch for longer
- Private: customer pins runtime image/tag and upgrades when they choose
Is that accurate?

Connor O'Brien: mostly. nuance: Hosted “LTS channel” likely means customers can opt into the LTS runtime line (esp if they’re on Dedicated/Enterprise hosted). For pure self-serve hosted we may not expose “LTS” as a selectable channel immediately. but for enterprise hosted / dedicated yes.

Soojin Lee: For FAQ audience (CSMs), we can phrase as “Availability depends on deployment mode + contract; talk to your CSM/TAM.” but keep the core promise consistent.

Rachel Kim: Draft language attempt (please edit):
Q: What is Runtime LTS?
A: Runtime LTS is a stable, long-lived release line of the Redwood serving runtime designed for enterprise environments. LTS prioritizes kernel + scheduling stability, predictable patch cadence, and auditable artifacts. LTS includes critical fixes and security patches backported to a fixed baseline; it does not include all new features from mainline.

Jasmine Liu: add “recommended for Dedicated + Private customers with change control / validation requirements”

Connor O'Brien: + mention “reproducible builds / signed artifacts + checksums” somewhere (esp for Private).

Liam O'Rourke: For Private pinning, customers will ask “what exactly do i pin?”
Answer should say:
- runtime image tag (e.g. runtime:1.18.2-lts)
- Helm values field / installer config option
- checksums/provenance doc
- rollback = pin previous patch + redeploy, and keep last-known-good in registry

Talia Benson: I’ll add that plus link to the Private upgrade/rollback guide once it’s published.

Dev Patel: Security FAQ wording suggestion:
“LTS receives security fixes that impact the runtime and its shipped dependencies when they meet Redwood’s severity thresholds. For critical issues we ship an out-of-band LTS patch. Customers will receive advisories with impacted versions, mitigation guidance, and fixed versions.”
We should avoid promising a specific hour-based SLA in the FAQ unless security signs off.

Connor O'Brien: +1. we have internal target (e.g. 72h for critical) but not ready as public promise. say “expedited” and “communicated via advisory.”

Avery Johnson: please include a clean “What qualifies for a backport?” section with examples. they want to know if perf-only qualifies.

Connor O'Brien: propose examples:
Eligible:
- Sev1 crash (e.g. KV cache compaction crash)
- correctness bug w/ customer-visible wrong outputs
- security fixes
- scheduler starvation causing request timeouts (if severity threshold met)
Not eligible:
- net-new features
- model onboarding
- refactors
- perf optimizations unless they are required to remediate a severe regression introduced in the LTS line itself

Hannah Schmitt: wording for “perf regressions” is important. customers worry about “you’ll ship a patch that slows us down.”

Connor O'Brien: we can add: “All LTS patches are gated on performance regression thresholds across canonical workloads; any known perf tradeoffs are called out in release notes.”

Rachel Kim: adding question:
Q: Will LTS patches change performance?
A: LTS is designed to minimize performance variance. Every patch runs through Redwood’s performance gate suite; we aim to keep perf within defined thresholds. If a patch contains a known perf tradeoff (rare), we’ll document it and provide mitigations/rollback guidance.

Soojin Lee: add “thresholds vary by workload/GPU; we report results at p50/p95 + throughput” (CSMs can say “we have benchmarks” without dumping raw numbers).

Liam O'Rourke: Another Q from platform teams: “How do we know what we’re running?”
Answer: “Each LTS artifact maps to a git commit + build provenance; release notes include the tag; artifacts have checksums/signatures.”

Jasmine Liu: Add “where do release notes live and what format?” Customers want CVE format.

Connor O'Brien: LTS release notes format includes: Summary, Security, Fixes, Perf, Known issues, Upgrade notes, Compatibility matrix. CVEs get a dedicated line item w/ impacted versions + fixed version.

Talia Benson: ok consolidating. Proposed FAQ bullets (CSM internal):
- Support window: “Each LTS line has a published support window (target ~12 months).”
- Patch cadence: “Monthly patches + out-of-band security fixes.”
- Backport policy: “Security + Sev1/Sev2 correctness only, minimal diffs, approvals required.”
- Request process: “Open Support ticket w/ required diagnostics; CSM/TAM can escalate via #eng-releases if Sev1.”

Dev Patel: Please be explicit: “CSMs should not promise acceptance of a backport request.” we can say “we will evaluate” and give criteria.

Avery Johnson: Can we get one paragraph “customer-facing commitment language” for AEs/CSMs?

Soojin Lee: Draft:
“Redwood offers a Runtime LTS channel for customers who need a stable serving runtime baseline. LTS provides a predictable patch cadence (typically monthly) and a clear backport policy focused on security and critical correctness fixes. LTS prioritizes stability over rapid feature delivery, with slower-change release notes and auditable artifacts to support enterprise change management.”

Connor O'Brien: looks good. I’d tweak “typically monthly” -> “monthly” (unless we think we’ll miss it). I’m comfortable committing to monthly once GA.

Rachel Kim: I’ll keep it as “monthly” for pilot docs but add “pilot cadence may vary while we validate process” as internal note.

Hannah Schmitt: question: “Are patches mandatory?”

Connor O'Brien: default: optional; but we can label “recommended” or “mandatory” if it fixes Sev1/security. If mandatory, we’ll include explicit upgrade guidance + timelines (esp Dedicated/Hosted).

Jasmine Liu: support wants a simple flag:
- Mandatory: security/actively exploited, Sev1 crash w/ no workaround
- Recommended: high-impact correctness w/ workaround
- Optional: minor fixes

Talia Benson: great. I’ll add to FAQ as internal guidance.

Liam O'Rourke: Also add “How do i validate before upgrading?”
Answer: “run staging smoke tests + Redwood-provided validation checklist; we can provide perf report links per patch.”

Rachel Kim: Action items:
- Rachel: consolidate thread into FAQ doc + share for review
- Connor: sanity-check technical wording (support window, eligibility)
- Dev/Jasmine: provide ticket template snippet
- Soojin: final polish for customer-friendly language

Connor O'Brien: :thumbsup: tag me when draft is ready.

Dev Patel: I’ll paste support template in the doc tonight.

Soojin Lee: will tighten phrasing + make sure we don’t accidentally promise SLAs.

Hannah Schmitt: thanks all — this will help a ton on calls next week.
